title: Quantifying cell shape and density fluctuations in epithelial tissue in vivo
authors: Jake Turley, Helen Weavers, Paul Martin, Isaac V. Chenchiah, Tanniemola B. Liverpool
abstract: Controlling changes in cell shape are crucial for many biological processes, such as tissue development and wound healing. Tissues typically are heterogeneous with a variety of cell shapes and sizes. Of particular interest are local deviations from an average cell shape and size. These fluctuations may extend and transmit across tissues, potentially offering valuable insights into tissue characteristics such as variations in effective "stiffness" or rigidity. In this study, we present a theoretical framework that captures the dynamics of epithelial cell shapes within tissue, incorporating both their average behaviour and fluctuation patterns. We model cells as interacting soft ellipsoids of varying size and aspect ratio. Coarse-graining our model, we obtain a set of continuum stochastic differential equations from which we derive spatial-temporal correlation functions. These correlation functions fit with our experimental data from the developmental process of the \textit{Drosophila} pupal wing. From the correlation functions, critical parameters representing active cell shape changes and effective tissue "stiffness" can be determined.
summary: This work develops a theoretical framework to analyze cell shape and density fluctuations in living epithelial tissues. By coarse-graining microscopic cell interactions into continuum stochastic equations, the authors quantify how active remodeling and passive stiffness govern tissue mechanics. The results demonstrate that these parameters can be extracted from measured correlation functions, providing quantitative insights into biological processes like wound healing.
main_problem: The study quantifies cell shape and density fluctuations in epithelial tissue in vivo to gain insights into the underlying mechanical properties, such as effective tissue stiffness.
main_result: The theoretical framework successfully distinguishes between active cell shape remodeling and passive tissue stiffness, showing that active remodeling is crucial for rapid wound healing.
method: The authors developed a theoretical framework by coarse-graining microscopic equations of motion into continuum stochastic differential equations, allowing for the derivation of spatial-temporal correlation functions.
model_or_system: The system is epithelial tissue, modeled by interacting soft ellipsoids. The dynamics are described by continuum fields for local cell density ($\hat{ho}$) and cell shape ($\hat{\mathbf{Q}}$), derived from microscopic interactions.
key_observables: Cell density correlation function ($C_{hoho}$), cell shape correlation function ($C_{qq}$), and derived parameters like active remodeling strength ($A$) and effective stiffness ($L$).
important_parameters: Active shape change parameter ($A$), effective tissue stiffness ($L$), cell density ($ho$), and mean $q$-tensor ($ ar{Q}$).
main_assumptions: The approach relies on linearization around mean fields and using leading-order terms in the continuum limit; it also assumes accurate measurement of cell shapes via deep learning.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate cell shape fluctuations in the *Drosophila* wing, show time evolution of mean density and shape parameters, and compare correlation decay rates in wild-type versus mutant tissues near wounds.
paper_structure: The paper moves from defining the physical problem and microscopic model to deriving continuum stochastic equations via coarse-graining. It then analyzes the resulting correlation functions to fit and extract key mechanical parameters ($A$ and $L$) by comparing predictions against experimental data from wounded and perturbed tissues.
why_interesting: While focused on biology, the mathematical machinery—deriving continuum stochastic equations and correlation functions from microscopic particle interactions—is highly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, active matter, and many-body dynamics in soft matter systems.
